title: Enquiries regarding EU funding for the Digital Freedom Fund and grants to the  Gesellschaft für Freiheitsrechte
text:
QUESTION

PE782.726v01-00
Question for written answer E-000002/2026
to the Commission
Rule 144
Alexander Jungbluth (ESN)
Subject:
Enquiries regarding EU funding for the Digital Freedom Fund and grants to the
Gesellschaft für Freiheitsrechte
The Digital Freedom Fund (DFF) receives funding for the digiRISE project (2022-2025) from
the EU’s Citizens, Equality, Rights and Values programme, which it says is used to support
processes that safeguard digital rights. The Gesellschaft für Freiheitsrechte (Society for Civil
Rights, GFF) has been funded by the DFF since 2018, receiving an estimated total of EUR
400 0001 for projects in areas such as digital rights, migration and algorithm transparency.
The GFF also uses the funding to bring legal action against political opponents2 or
governments3. In its reply to written question E-002215/2025, the Commission confirmed that
funding had been granted to the DFF for digiRISE, but explicitly stated that: ‘The project
does not foresee the possibility of redistributing EU funding to third parties.’4 That statement
contradicts the facts set out above.
1.
What does the Commission mean by ‘redistributing EU funding to third parties’ in this
specific context?
2.
How does the Commission ensure that EU funding for digiRISE does not free up or
complement private funding of the DFF (‘fungibility’) to finance other, potentially
politically sensitive, GFF activities such as legal action against governments of EU
Member States?
3.
Does the Commission take the view that EU funding for the DFF – which supports the
GFF with strategic litigation in the abovementioned areas – is compatible with the
principle of political neutrality of EU funding, even if the support concerned is indirect?
Submitted: 2.1.2026
1
https://freiheitsrechte.org/en/ueber-die-gff/finanzen-transparenz.
2
https://freiheitsrechte.org/spende-afd-gutachten.
3
https://freiheitsrechte.org/ueber-die-gff/presse/pressemitteilungen-der-gesellschaft-fur-freiheitsrechte/pm-
spyware-anzeige.
4
https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-10-2025-002215-ASW_EN.html

--- ANSWER ---

EN
E-000002/2026
Answer given by Mr McGrath
on behalf of the European Commission
(20.2.2026)
The Financial Support to Third Parties provided for in the Financial Regulation1 allows, if
expressly foreseen in the grant agreement, the beneficiaries to provide financial support to
entities that are not part to the grant agreement. This is possible if done in line with the
provisions of the Financial Regulation. The DigiRise project does not foresee this possibility
to redistribute funding.
The DigiRise project is funded through an action grant, whereby funding is provided to
implement the project described in the agreement. The costs of implementing the action are
set out in a budget that is part of the grant agreement. The grant is paid to the beneficiaries
only if the action is implemented in line with the agreement, if the foreseen activities are
implemented and the deliverables approved by the Commission. Funding cannot be used for
other purposes that the ones listed in the grant agreement.
The general objective of the Citizens, Equality, Rights and Values (CERV)2 funding
programme adopted by the EU Member States in the Council and by the European Parliament
is to protect and promote rights and values as enshrined in the Treaties and the Charter of
Fundamental Rights. Funding is provided in full transparency and in line with the Financial
Regulation after a highly competitive process following open calls published on the Funding
and Tender portal. Proposals are evaluated against award criteria such as quality and
relevance in order to make sure that they implement the objectives of the funding programme.
1 Regulation (EU, Euratom) 2024/2509 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 23 September 2024 on
the financial rules applicable to the general budget of the Union (recast) ELI:
http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/2509/oj.
2 Regulation (EU) 2021/692 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 28 April 2021 establishing the
Citizens, Equality, Rights and Values Programme and repealing Regulation (EU) No 1381/2013 of the European
Parliament and of the Council and Council Regulation (EU) No 390/2014 ELI:
http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2021/692/oj.

title: EU financial assistance for the Palestinian Authority
text:
QUESTION

PE780.405v01-00
Question for written answer E-000003/2026
to the Commission
Rule 144
Bert-Jan Ruissen (ECR), Lukas Mandl (PPE), Alice Teodorescu Måwe (PPE), Fernand
Kartheiser (NI), Aurelijus Veryga (ECR), Charlie Weimers (ECR), Beatrice Timgren
(ECR), Dick Erixon (ECR), Sander Smit (PPE), Sebastian Tynkkynen (ECR), Hildegard
Bentele (PPE)
Subject:
EU financial assistance for the Palestinian Authority
Following the July 2024 Letter of Intent between the Palestinian Authority (PA) and the
European Commission, the Commission repeatedly stated that the EU’s financial assistance
for the PA would be linked to verifiable progress made in education reform, including the
revision of textbooks to align them fully with UNESCO standards, with grade 12 to be
reformed by the end of 2024 and grades 1-4 by September 2025.
However, in recent replies1 to written questions the Commission has referred generally to the
PA’s ‘continuous’ internal review processes, without specifying whether the PA has met these
specific date-bound commitments. Independent assessments indicate that newly issued PA
textbooks and the online Gaza curriculum replicate the same content previously identified as
problematic.
1.
Has the Commission formally revised or replaced the original reform benchmarks
contained in the July 2024 Letter of Intent2? If so, what new benchmarks has it adopted
and on what grounds?
2.
What specific documentary evidence of textbook reform3 has the Commission received
since July 2024, and how does this confirm progress made toward UNESCO-aligned
reform?
3.
In cases where the PA’s new textbooks or abridged Gaza curriculum are found to
reproduce unreformed content, what are the consequences under the conditionality
framework, and will the Commission suspend or adjust future disbursements until
verifiable reform is demonstrated?
Submitted: 5.1.2026
1
E-001465/2025 (https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-10-2025-001465_EN.html) and E-
003064/2025 (https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-10-2025-003064_EN.html).
2
E.g. reform deadlines for grade 12 and grades 1-4.
3
E.g. revised textbooks and independent verification.

--- ANSWER ---

(English version)
Question for written answer E-000003/26
to the Commission
Bert-Jan Ruissen (ECR), Lukas Mandl (PPE), Alice Teodorescu Måwe (PPE), Fernand Kartheiser (NI), Aurelijus
Veryga (ECR), Charlie Weimers (ECR), Beatrice Timgren (ECR), Dick Erixon (ECR), Sander Smit (PPE), Sebastian
Tynkkynen (ECR), Hildegard Bentele (PPE)
(5 January 2026)
Subject: EU financial assistance for the Palestinian Authority
Following the July 2024 Letter of Intent between the Palestinian Authority (PA) and the European Commission, the
Commission repeatedly stated that the EU’s financial assistance for the PA would be linked to verifiable progress made in
education reform, including the revision of textbooks to align them fully with Unesco standards, with grade 12 to be reformed
by the end of 2024 and grades 1-4 by September 2025.
However, in recent replies (1) to written questions the Commission has referred generally to the PA’s ‘continuous’ internal
review processes, without specifying whether the PA has met these specific date-bound commitments. Independent assessments
indicate that newly issued PA textbooks and the online Gaza curriculum replicate the same content previously identified as
problematic.
1.
Has the Commission formally revised or replaced the original reform benchmarks contained in the July 2024 Letter of
Intent (2)? If so, what new benchmarks has it adopted and on what grounds?
2.
What specific documentary evidence of textbook reform (3) has the Commission received since July 2024, and how does
this confirm progress made toward Unesco-aligned reform?
3.
In cases where the PA’s new textbooks or abridged Gaza curriculum are found to reproduce unreformed content, what are
the consequences under the conditionality framework, and will the Commission suspend or adjust future disbursements until
verifiable reform is demonstrated?
Submitted: 5.1.2026
Answer given by Ms Šuica on behalf of the European Commission
(8 April 2026)
In the Letter of Intent between the Palestinian Authority (PA) and the Commission dated July 2024 (1), the PA committed to
undertake substantial and credible reforms including for the education sector, with a focus on improving the quality of the
education system that encompasses the development of educational materials and high-quality teaching and learning.
The annex to the Letter of Intent listed the adoption by the PA of an action plan to improve quality education as key progress
indicator by the end of August 2024. The said action plan was adopted in mid-August.
In the following months, the PA developed, in coordination with the EU, a Joint EU-PA Reform Matrix that included a
sequencing of clear benchmarks, as the basis for disbursements under the Multiannual and Comprehensive Support Programme
for recovery and resilience for 2025-2027.
The Reform Matrix agreed by the PA and the EU in November 2024 included milestones focusing on the education reform.
These milestones complement and upgrade the benchmarks contained in the Letter of Intent.
The PA President, at the UN General Assembly in September 2025, reiterated the commitment to fully transition to learning
materials aligned to UN Educational, Scientific, and Cultural Organisation (Unesco) standards within the next two years.
The PA has made initial revisions to grade 12 and more comprehensive revisions to grades one to four to align with Unesco
standards.
Revised learning material in the format of ‘educational packages’ has been published on the Palestinian Ministry of Education
website in December 2024 and October 2025 respectively.
Substantial changes in the curriculum for grades one to four have been noted and revisions are currently being assessed by
experts contracted by the Commission.
1
E-001465/2025 (https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-10-2025-001465_EN.html) and E-003064/2025
(https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-10-2025-003064_EN.html).
2
E.g. reform deadlines for grade 12 and grades 1-4.
3
E.g. revised textbooks and independent verification.

The EU remains engaged with the PA on curriculum and broader education sector reform and EU disbursements are linked to
the PA’s achievement of key reforms identified in the Reform Matrix.

title: Protected Disclosure Directive
text:
QUESTION

PE780.408v01-00
Question for written answer E-000005/2026
to the Commission
Rule 144
Kathleen Funchion (The Left)
Subject:
Protected Disclosure Directive
Ireland passed the Protected Disclosures (Amendment) Act 20221, which came into effect on
1 January 2023, thus transposing the Protected Disclosure Directive2.
Many people who have made such disclosures still raise issues they face in Ireland with
protected disclosures. In many instances, these issues have been raised in Parliament level via
the Committee on Petitions.
1.
Is the Commission aware of cases being brought to the Committee on Petitions calling
into question the application of the Protected Disclosure Directive?
2.
Does the Commission have any comment on Ireland’s application of the Protected
Disclosure Directive?
3.
What avenues does the Commission advise people to take should they feel the Protected
Disclosure Directive is not being properly or fairly applied to their case?
Submitted: 5.1.2026
1
https://www.oireachtas.ie/en/bills/bill/2022/17/.
2
Directive (EU) 2019/1937 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 23 October 2019 on the
protection of persons who report breaches of Union law (OJ L 305, 26.11.2019, p. 17, ELI:
http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2019/1937/oj).

--- ANSWER ---

EN
E-000005/2026
Answer given by Mr McGrath
on behalf of the European Commission
(19.2.2026)
The Commission is aware of cases relating to the implementation of Directive (EU)
2019/1937 on the protection of persons who report breaches of EU law1 being brought to the
attention of the Committee on Petitions of the European Parliament.
The Commission opened infringement proceedings against Ireland2 on 27 January 2022 for
failure to notify transposition measures for the Directive. Following these proceedings,
Ireland notified the relevant measures to the Commission. After assessing these measures and
confirming they ensure the complete transposition of the Directive’s requirements, the
Commission decided on 16 November 2023 to close the infringement proceedings against
Ireland.
The Commission is monitoring the correct implementation of the Directive in all Member
States, including Ireland.
The Commission monitors the situation in the Member States and aims to follow up on
systemic issues involving the application of EU law. It is for the national authorities,
including national courts, to analyse individual cases in light of the national legal framework
providing for whistleblower protection, and to ensure that citizens' rights under EU law are
protected.
1 Directive (EU) 2019/1937 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 23 October 2019 on the protection
of persons who report breaches of Union law, 26.11.2019, OJ L 305, p. 17–56
2 INFR(2022)0098, see specific webpage on infringements https://ec.europa.eu/implementing-eu-law/search-
infringement-
decisions/?lang_code=en&langCode=EN&version=v1&typeOfSearch=byDecision&refId=INFR(2022)0098&dg
=JUST&policyArea=JUST-123&memberState=IE&page=1&size=10&order=desc&sortColumns=decisionDate.

title: Publication of people’s real-time geolocation data under Spain’s compulsory V16 system
text:
QUESTION

PE780.976v01-00
Question for written answer E-000006/2026
to the Commission
Rule 144
Alvise Pérez (NI)
Subject:
Publication of people’s real-time geolocation data under Spain’s compulsory V16
system
Spanish legislation requires the use of connected V16 devices to indicate vehicles that have
broken down or are stopped on the public highway. The devices also transmit geolocation
data to systems managed by the Directorate-General for Traffic.
Real-time location information is publicly available on a web-based map – access is
unrestricted and no login is required. As a result, anyone can look up the location of people
who find themselves in potentially vulnerable situations.
While national authorities argue that data is ‘anonymised’, exact and real-time geolocation
can constitute personal data when it indirectly enables natural persons to be identified or
poses a risk to their safety.
In light of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (General Data Protection Regulation):
1.
Does the Commission believe that a Member State making real-time geolocation
information provided under a mandatory system is consistent with the GDPR?
2.
Is the mere claim of anonymisation enough, when the precise nature of the data
indirectly allows a person to be identified or could generate risks?
3.
Would such processing necessarily require a data protection impact assessment and
restriction of access strictly to competent authorities? Does the Commission intend to
request information from the Spanish authorities regarding the applicable legal basis
and safeguards?
Submitted: 5.1.2026

title: Provisional tariffs imposed by China on EU dairy products
text:
QUESTION

PE780.977v01-00
Question for written answer E-000007/2026
to the Commission
Rule 144
Daniel Buda (PPE)
Subject:
Provisional tariffs imposed by China on EU dairy products
The Chinese authorities have recently introduced provisional tariffs of between 21.9 % and
42.7 % on certain dairy products from the EU as part of an anti-subsidy investigation
launched in August 2024, with the final decision to be adopted in February 2026. These
measures follow the introduction of five-year tariffs on pig meat imports from the EU, which
has increased the economic pressure on EU producers and the agri-food chain, especially in
Member States for which China constitutes a significant export market.
Given these circumstances:
1.
How does the Commission view the cumulative impact of the tariffs applied by China,
first in the pig meat sector and now in the dairy sector, on EU farmers and processors?
2.
What kinds of response is the Commission preparing in the run-up to China's final
decision, to be adopted in February 2026?
3.
Given that, after these issues with the USA and now with China, ever more EU
agricultural producers are losing access to major external markets, what action will the
Commission take to prevent the emergence of adverse structural effects on farmers’
incomes and on the competitiveness of the EU agri-food sector?
Submitted: 5.1.2026

--- ANSWER ---

EN
E-000007/2026
Answer given by Mr Šefčovič
on behalf of the European Commission
(17.2.2026)
The Commission is aware of the importance of these cases for both the European dairy and
pig meat sectors and has intervened in these investigations from the start in support of the
industries and Member States concerned. The EU has been using all means at its disposal to
defend EU farmers and processors confronted with the abusive use of trade defence
instruments, notably by taking action at the World Trade Organization (WTO) against China’s
initiation of the anti-subsidy investigation on dairy. While the impact of the measures will be
significant, it is too early to quantify in terms of trade impact since the additional duties from
China have been imposed recently.
As regards the concluded investigation on pork, the Commission’s interventions together with
those of industry and Member States have achieved a reduction of the definitive measures
compared to the provisional measures imposed.
Concerning the ongoing dairy investigation, the Commission, in close cooperation with the
Member States and the dairy industry submitted comments throughout the proceeding and
also in reaction to the final determination issued on 30 January. It is noted that the final duties
proposed are lower than the provisional duties. Nevertheless, the Commission considers that
the whole investigation and the duties are unwarranted and will now consider any further
steps.
The Commission will explore all options to protect the interests of the EU industry, also in
view of the compliance by China with its obligations as member of the WTO.
The Commission will continue to monitor the economic impact of the Chinese duties on the
affected sectors in the EU. If needed, steps may be taken to respond to market disturbances
through EU measures financed under the agricultural reserve.

title: Impact of LULUCF Regulation on the availability of horticultural peat
text:
QUESTION

PE780.978v01-00
Question for written answer E-000008/2026
to the Commission
Rule 144
Hilde Vautmans (Renew), Olivier Chastel (Renew), Benoit Cassart (Renew)
Subject:
Impact of LULUCF Regulation on the availability of horticultural peat
Peat is crucial for European greenhouse growers, supporting the production of vegetables,
fruit, mushrooms, ornamental plants and tree seedlings. It is foundational to resource-efficient
greenhouse horticulture, reducing the need for water, fertilisers and pesticides, while ensuring
high-yield harvests. Peat enables the use of other organic materials such as bark and wood
fibre. Without reliable access to horticultural peat, European growers face higher costs, lower
output, and diminished global competitiveness. As a domestic resource, peat enhances the
EU’s strategic autonomy by reducing reliance on imported growing media. Just 0.2 % of the
EU’s peatlands are used for horticultural peat production.
Existing greenhouse gas models under the LULUCF Regulation1 do not accurately account
for horticultural peat, treating it similarly to energy peat despite differences in usage,
decomposition and post-use impact. This misclassification threatens the availability of peat
for horticultural use.
To ensure the continued availability of horticultural peat, it is essential that the Commission
scientifically evaluates the emissions of all growing media and maintains access to this critical
agricultural input.
1.
How will the Commission ensure the LULUCF Regulation does not harm horticultural
peat production?
2.
Will the Commission revise greenhouse gas emission models to differentiate
horticultural peat from energy peat?
3.
How will the Commission support indoor horticulture and inputs like horticultural peat
in future policies?
Submitted: 5.1.2026
1
Regulation (EU) 2018/841 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 30 May 2018 on the inclusion of
greenhouse gas emissions and removals from land use, land use change and forestry in the 2030 climate and
energy framework (OJ L 156, 19.6.2018, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2018/841/oj).

--- ANSWER ---

(English version)
Question for written answer E-000008/26
to the Commission
Hilde Vautmans (Renew), Olivier Chastel (Renew), Benoit Cassart (Renew)
(5 January 2026)
Subject: Impact of LULUCF Regulation on the availability of horticultural peat
Peat is crucial for European greenhouse growers, supporting the production of vegetables, fruit, mushrooms, ornamental plants
and tree seedlings. It is foundational to resource-efficient greenhouse horticulture, reducing the need for water, fertilisers and
pesticides, while ensuring high-yield harvests. Peat enables the use of other organic materials such as bark and wood fibre.
Without reliable access to horticultural peat, European growers face higher costs, lower output, and diminished global
competitiveness. As a domestic resource, peat enhances the EU’s strategic autonomy by reducing reliance on imported growing
media. Just 0.2% of the EU’s peatlands are used for horticultural peat production.
Existing greenhouse gas models under the LULUCF Regulation (1) do not accurately account for horticultural peat, treating it
similarly to energy peat despite differences in usage, decomposition and post-use impact. This misclassification threatens the
availability of peat for horticultural use.
To ensure the continued availability of horticultural peat, it is essential that the Commission scientifically evaluates the
emissions of all growing media and maintains access to this critical agricultural input.
1.
How will the Commission ensure the LULUCF Regulation does not harm horticultural peat production?
2.
Will the Commission revise greenhouse gas emission models to differentiate horticultural peat from energy peat?
3.
How will the Commission support indoor horticulture and inputs like horticultural peat in future policies?
Submitted: 5.1.2026
Answer given by Mr Hoekstra on behalf of the European Commission
(6 March 2026)
1.
Regulation (EU) 841/2018 (1) sets an EU-wide net removals target in 2030, aiming to increase the EU’s net removals by
about 15% and reverse declining trends. This EU target means that Members States must meet binding net carbon removal
national targets, leading to a better performance of the Land Use, Land-Use Change and Forestry (LULUCF) sector. Member
States are responsible for implementing the appropriate policies and measures to achieve these targets.
2.
The accounting of greenhouse gas emissions and removals across all sectors, including LULUCF, are based on the
Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Guidelines (2) as adopted by the Conference of the Parties to the United
Nations Convention on Climate Change or the Conference of the Parties serving as the Meeting of the Parties to the Paris
Agreement.
3.
While the Commission advocates for protecting and rewetting of peatlands, as an effective way to curb greenhouse gas
emissions and increasing resilience towards the risks of floods, droughts, and fires, the replacement of peat with other materials
can pose challenges in the horticultural sector. To take account of such challenges, the Commission is for example considering
specific provisions regarding the use of peat in growing media under the afforestation methodology currently under discussion
in the Expert Group on Carbon Removals in the context of the regulation (EU) 2024/3012 (3).

title: Increasing use of delegated acts and decline in parliamentary scrutiny
text:
QUESTION

PE776.156v01-00
Question for written answer E-000011/2026
to the Commission
Rule 144
Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE)
Subject:
Increasing use of delegated acts and decline in parliamentary scrutiny
For several years now, the Commission has been making increasing use of the delegated acts
provided for in Article 290 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, including
in sensitive areas that have an impact on Member States’ competences or the institutional
balance. The proliferation of these acts raises serious questions around democratic scrutiny,
insofar as the European Parliament and national parliaments have limited scope to examine
their content, desirability and specific legal repercussions.
This practice contributes to a gradual transfer of legislative decisions to the Commission,
without any in-depth legislative debate or explicit consent by the general public, and it
undermines the separation of powers within the Union.
In view of the above:
1.
What objective criteria does the Commission apply when deciding whether to use a
delegated act or the ordinary legislative procedure?
2.
How does it rationalise the effects of these acts on areas that fall mainly within national
competences, without any real scrutiny by national parliaments?
3.
Does it plan to strengthen the parliamentary scrutiny mechanisms – including through
an extended right of veto or longer scrutiny periods – to ensure that Member States’
sovereignty is respected?
Submitted: 5.1.2026

title: Artificial intelligence to counter false claims by minor asylum seekers
text:
QUESTION

PE776.157v01-00
Question for written answer E-000012/2026
to the Commission
Rule 144
Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE)
Subject:
Artificial intelligence to counter false claims by minor asylum seekers
Eurostat figures show that the European Union registered 234 670 first-time asylum seekers
under the age of 18 in 2024 – 25.7 % of the total number. Of those, 15.9 % were
unaccompanied minors1.
A number of countries have found that a considerable proportion of minor declarations are not
confirmed by assessments. Belgian authorities report that 2 345 asylum seekers in 2024 were
self-declared unaccompanied minors. After assessment, 823 of those were classified as adults,
although not all age assessments have been completed yet2. Of the applicants for international
protection claiming to be unaccompanied minors, 86.1 % are boys.
In Austria, 489 age assessments were carried out in 2023; 275 (56.2 %) concluded that the
applicant was not under 18. In 2024, 214 assessments were carried out, 111 of which
concluded that the applicant was not under 183.
Given the extent of the issue, the UK Government plans to use artificial intelligence and facial
recognition to estimate the age of migrants whose identity is not known. This quick and
reliable technology is already used for online age checks.
1.
Does the Commission collect or can it publish comparable EU-level statistics on age
disputes and the outcome thereof?
2.
Will the Commission propose a minimum EU standard (quality, timeframe, checks,
channels for appeal) to prevent adults being placed with children?
3.
Does the Commission intend to integrate artificial intelligence into checks on asylum
seekers’ ages?
Submitted: 5.1.2026
1
https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php/Children_in_migration_-_asylum_applicants
2
https://www.cgrs.be/en/news/asylum-statistics-survey-2024?
3
https://asylumineurope.org/reports/country/austria/asylum-procedure/guarantees-vulnerable-
groups/identification/?

--- ANSWER ---

EN
E-000012/2026
Answer given by Mr Brunner
on behalf of the European Commission
(18.3.2026)
There are no comparable EU-level statistics available on the number of age assessment
procedures carried out in the Member States and their outcomes. Regulation (EU) 862/2007
on statistics on migration and international protection1, as amended in June 20202, does not
require Member States to report such data.
Regulation (EU) 2024/13483 provides that, where there are doubts as to whether or not an
applicant is a minor, the determining authority may undertake a multi-disciplinary assessment,
including a psychosocial assessment, which should be carried out by qualified professionals
and should not be based solely on the applicant’s physical appearance or behaviour. The
multi-disciplinary assessment should be carried out in a manner that gives primary
consideration to the best interests of the child. When inconclusive, it may be followed with a
medical examination, to be carried out with full respect for the individual’s dignity. The
results from the medical examination and the multi-disciplinary assessment should be
analysed together. Where the result of the age assessment is not conclusive or includes an
age-range starting from below 18 years, Regulation (EU) 2024/1348 requires Member States
to assume that the applicant is a minor.
The Asylum and Migration Management Strategy4 emphasises the importance of deploying
and using new technologies, including AI tools, to provide Member States with modern,
secure and efficient tools to improve the quality, consistency and timeliness of decision
making. In line with the existing regulatory requirements, the Commission plans to set up a
Forum for AI on Migration to identify the possible uses of AI.
1 Regulation (EC) 862/2007 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 July 2007 on Community
statistics on migration and international protection and repealing Council Regulation (EEC) No 311/76 on the
compilation of statistics on foreign workers (OJ L 199, 31.7.2007, pp. 23–29 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-
content/EN/ALL/?uri=CELEX:32007R0862).
2 Consolidated text: Regulation (EC) 862/2007 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 July 2007
on Community statistics on migration and international protection and repealing Council Regulation (EEC)
311/76 on the compilation of statistics on foreign workers: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2007/862/2021-07-
01/eng.

title: The Commission’s persistent failure to monitor NGO funding and ideological risks
text:
QUESTION

PE780.252v01-00
Question for written answer E-000013/2026
to the Commission
Rule 144
Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE)
Subject:
The Commission’s persistent failure to monitor NGO funding and ideological
risks
The European Court of Auditors’ Special Report 11/20251 paints a grim picture: the
Commission is unable to ensure reliable and comprehensive transparency with regard to
funding paid to NGOs, despite repeated warnings over several years. This chronic lack of
oversight is therefore neither isolated nor accidental, but structural.
This is all the more worrying given that EU funding has already been provided to NGOs
accused of being close to the Muslim Brotherhood (CLAIM Allianz), including through
programmes such as Erasmus+ (Al Sharq Forum), which has led to serious concerns being
raised in several Member States. The lack of proactive oversight, combined with unclear
definitions of NGOs and an over-reliance on self-declaration, fuels the suspicion that EU
public funding is being used in an ideological and militant manner.
1.
Does the Commission intend to introduce binding agreements which make the payment
of EU funding conditional on beneficiaries undertaking to refrain from taking any
partisan or political position?
2.
What criteria and checks does it apply before granting EU funds so as to exclude
organisations whose ideological, political or financial links give rise to serious
questions?
3.
Does it intend to set up clear exclusion and sanction mechanisms – including the
suspension or repayment of funding – to deal with NGOs that pose security risks to
Member States?
Submitted: 5.1.2026
1
https://www.eca.europa.eu/ECAPublications/SR-2025-11/SR-2025-11_EN.pdf

--- ANSWER ---

(English version)
Question for written answer E-000013/26
to the Commission
Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE)
(5 January 2026)
Subject: The Commission’s persistent failure to monitor NGO funding and ideological risks
The European Court of Auditors’ Special Report 11/2025 (1) paints a grim picture: the Commission is unable to ensure reliable
and comprehensive transparency with regard to funding paid to NGOs, despite repeated warnings over several years. This
chronic lack of oversight is therefore neither isolated nor accidental, but structural.
This is all the more worrying given that EU funding has already been provided to NGOs accused of being close to the Muslim
Brotherhood (CLAIM Allianz), including through programmes such as Erasmus+ (Al Sharq Forum), which has led to serious
concerns being raised in several Member States. The lack of proactive oversight, combined with unclear definitions of NGOs
and an over-reliance on self-declaration, fuels the suspicion that EU public funding is being used in an ideological and militant
manner.
1.
Does the Commission intend to introduce binding agreements which make the payment of EU funding conditional on
beneficiaries undertaking to refrain from taking any partisan or political position?
2.
What criteria and checks does it apply before granting EU funds so as to exclude organisations whose ideological,
political or financial links give rise to serious questions?
3.
Does it intend to set up clear exclusion and sanction mechanisms — including the suspension or repayment of funding —
to deal with NGOs that pose security risks to Member States?
Submitted: 5.1.2026
Answer given by Mr Serafin on behalf of the European Commission
(27 March 2026)
EU funding is awarded based on clear eligibility, exclusion, selection and award criteria.
The award of EU funds is conditional on the absence of any exclusion grounds laid down in Article 138 of the Financial
Regulation (1), including where an applicant for a grant has engaged in activities contrary to the EU founding values (2), fraud,
criminal organisation, terrorist offences and related activities, etc.
Before award and during the implementation of a grant, as well as before disbursing payments, participants and recipients of
EU funds and their affiliates are systematically checked against the Early Detection and Exclusion System database of the
Commission which contains a list of all excluded persons and entities.
Moreover, Article 14 of the Commission’s horizontal model grant agreement (3) requires beneficiaries to respect EU values.
The Commission will act immediately on evidence of non-compliance by implementing appropriate measures against
unreliable entities, such as the suspension of contract or payments, contract termination, recovery or exclusion from EU
financing.
All entities receiving or implementing EU funds are verified to ensure that they are not subject to the EU sanctions (4). Any
entity sanctioned by such measures is prohibited from receiving or implementing EU funds.
For participation in sensitive actions (e.g. defence, space, cybersecurity), entities, including non-governmental organisations,
are furthermore subject to the full set of measures in place to protect security or public order of the EU and its Member States.

title: Legal uncertainty imposed on national constitutional frameworks by a patchwork of European electoral rules
text:
QUESTION

PE766.438v01-00
Question for written answer E-000014/2026
to the Commission
Rule 144
Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE)
Subject:
Legal uncertainty imposed on national constitutional frameworks by a patchwork
of European electoral rules
Following the 2024 European elections, a number of institutions highlighted practical and
legal issues arising from the many EU rules on elections: the European Electoral Act, the
Digital Services Act, rules on political advertising and anti-disinformation mechanisms.
This patchwork of rules built around different legal bases undermines the clarity and legal
certainty of national constitutional frameworks, while organising elections is historically and
legally under within Member States’ competences. It also increases the risk of creating
conflicts between rules and transfers of competences without the people’s express consent.
Can the Commission say:
1.
What is the legal basis for this gradual broadening of EU rules into an area that
primarily falls within the scope of national constitutions?
2.
How does it intend to ensure these rules do not undermine the constitutional sovereignty
of Member States in electoral matters?
3.
Is it considering suspending or revising these arrangements to restore legal certainty in
line with national competences?
Submitted: 5.1.2026

--- ANSWER ---

(English version)
Question for written answer E-000014/26
to the Commission
Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE)
(5 January 2026)
Subject: Legal uncertainty imposed on national constitutional frameworks by a patchwork of European electoral rules
Following the 2024 European elections, a number of institutions highlighted practical and legal issues arising from the many
EU rules on elections: the European Electoral Act, the Digital Services Act, rules on political advertising and anti-
disinformation mechanisms.
This patchwork of rules built around different legal bases undermines the clarity and legal certainty of national constitutional
frameworks, while organising elections is historically and legally under within Member States’ competences. It also increases
the risk of creating conflicts between rules and transfers of competences without the people’s express consent.
Can the Commission say:
1.
What is the legal basis for this gradual broadening of EU rules into an area that primarily falls within the scope of
national constitutions?
2.
How does it intend to ensure these rules do not undermine the constitutional sovereignty of Member States in electoral
matters?
3.
Is it considering suspending or revising these arrangements to restore legal certainty in line with national competences?
Submitted: 5.1.2026
Answer given by Mr McGrath on behalf of the European Commission
(12 March 2026)
As enshrined in Articles 2 and 10 of the Treaty on European Union, democracy is a founding value on which the EU is built.
The Commission, together with all other EU institutions and the Member States, is responsible under the Treaties for promoting
the founding values of the EU, including democracy.
Free and fair elections are at the core of democracy. The conduct and organisation of elections are the competence and
responsibility of the Member States, in accordance with their constitutional and legislative rules, subject to EU law and their
international obligations.
For elections to the European Parliament, certain common principles are set out in the European Electoral Act (1), in line with
Article 223(1) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU).
The Political Advertising Regulation (2) and the Digital Services Act (3) have been adopted on the basis of Article 114 and
Article 16 TFEU, and Article 114 TFEU respectively, in full respect of the allocation of competences between the EU and
Member States. They do not regulate elections.
Instead, they establish common standards within the internal market for ensuring the transparency of political advertising and,
respectively, for ensuring that online platforms and search engines put in place measures to mitigate risks related to negative
effects on civic discourse and electoral processes.
The Commission is fully committed and actively engaged to help Member States in their efforts to ensure the fairness and
integrity of elections, including by supporting the application of this legislation.
The Council (4) also stressed the importance of maximising the use of EU tools, including the Political Advertising Regulation
and the Digital Services Act, to safeguard free and fair elections in the EU.

title: Enforcement of the Digital Services Act (DSA) – effective reporting channels, legal remedies and dispute settlement
text:
QUESTION

PE782.734v01-00
Question for written answer E-000017/2026
to the Commission
Rule 144
Pascal Arimont (PPE)
Subject:
Enforcement of the Digital Services Act (DSA) – effective reporting channels,
legal remedies and dispute settlement
In its report ‘Rights Without Reach – The DSA put to the test’1, HateAid examined how large
platforms such as YouTube, Facebook or X implement the key rights of the Digital Service
Act (DSA), in particular those laid down in Articles 16, 20 and 21. The investigation found,
among other things, that after exhausting all available legal remedies, only 57 % of reported
illegal content was removed during the project period. While 24 % of internal complaints
about a negative decision were successful in 2024, this figure fell to just 7.2 % in 2025.
Moreover, according to the report, excessive complexity, non-transparent structuring,
deterrent wording and targeted design elements systematically complicated the reporting of
illegal content. What is more, proceedings often remained without a decision for more than 90
or 180 days.
1.
What specific steps (including a timeline) is the Commission taking with regard to the
very large online platforms (VLOPs) concerned to ensure user-friendly reporting
channels that are clearly identifiable as DSA mechanisms, in accordance with Article 16
of the DSA?
2.
How does the Commission review and enforce the obligations to indicate when
decisions are automated (Article 16(6)) and the prohibition of making decisions on
complaints solely on the basis of automated means (Article 20(6))?
3.
Does the Commission intend to introduce guidelines and/or minimum standards on the
effectiveness of out-of-court dispute settlement under Article 21 (time limits,
justification, status information, implementation by platforms) and, if so, by when?
Submitted: 6.1.2026
1
https://hateaid.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/hateaid-dsa-rights-without-reach-2025.pdf

--- ANSWER ---

EN
E-000017/2026
Answer given by Executive Vice-President Virkkunen
on behalf of the European Commission
(26.2.2026)
The Commission and Digital Services Coordinators (DSCs) actively monitor the
implementation of the Digital Service Act (DSA)1, including compliance with Articles 16 and
20 by very large online platforms (VLOPs) and other providers of hosting services. Both the
Commission and DSCs have various supervisory powers at their disposal, including the power
to compel information from the providers. The Commission also continuously improves the
DSA transparency database to help inform this effort.
In October 2025, the Commission in addition adopted preliminary findings in relation to
Meta, concerning Facebook and Instagram, and a suspected breach of Articles 16(1) and 25(1)
DSA, as it appears to impose several unnecessary steps and additional demands on users and
to use deceptive interface designs. In December 2023, the Commission initiated proceedings
against the provider of X as it appears to fail to process notices on illegal content, to take
decisions in a diligent, non-arbitrary and objective manner and to notify individuals or entities
of the action taken in relation to notices. Both proceedings are still ongoing.
The Commission is closely monitoring the implementation of Article 21 of the DSA on out-
of-court dispute settlement (ODS) bodies. Under the DSA, ODS bodies must report on an
annual basis to the DSC that certified them. DSCs draw up a report on the functioning of the
ODS bodies they certified every two years. The Commission has commissioned a study to
identify and address the main issues faced by actors involved in the ODS process. This will
allow the Commission to have an accurate overview of the implementation of Article 21 and
assess whether additional guidance is needed.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/2065/oj/eng.

title: Impact of wind turbine noise on health: a blind spot in EU green policy
text:
QUESTION

PE782.736v01-00
Question for written answer E-000019/2026
to the Commission
Rule 144
Virginie Joron (PfE)
Subject:
Impact of wind turbine noise on health: a blind spot in EU green policy
Until now, accurately measuring the noise generated by wind turbines has been difficult.
However, on 12 November 2025, a study carried out by Uppsala University in Sweden
presented a high-fidelity simulation tool for more accurate acoustic modelling1. The results
show that ‘modern, large-scale wind turbines generate infrasound levels significantly higher
than those reported for older, smaller turbines.’
However, the current legal framework, and especially Directive 2002/49/EC relating to the
assessment and management of environmental noise, does not take into account this new
scientific data2.
1.
In light of these new scientific findings, does the Commission intend to revise Directive
2002/49/EC relating to the assessment and management of environmental noise in order
to include the effects of infrasound emitted by wind turbines?
2.
Does the Commission plan to support research, including through EU-funded
programmes, aimed at developing instruments allowing noise and infrasound pollution
linked to wind turbines to be measured and proven?
3.
Does the Commission intend to impose harmonised thresholds at EU level for noise and
infrasound emissions, given the potential impact of these emissions on public health
among people living nearby?
Submitted: 6.1.2026
1
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0003682X25006280?via%3Dihub
2
Directive 2002/49/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 25 June 2002 relating to the
assessment and management of environmental noise - Declaration by the Commission in the Conciliation
Committee on the Directive relating to the assessment and management of environmental noise.

--- ANSWER ---

(English version)
Question for written answer E-000019/26
to the Commission
Virginie Joron (PfE)
(6 January 2026)
Subject: Impact of wind turbine noise on health: a blind spot in EU green policy
Until now, accurately measuring the noise generated by wind turbines has been difficult. However, on 12 November 2025, a
study carried out by Uppsala University in Sweden presented a high-fidelity simulation tool for more accurate acoustic
modelling (1). The results show that ‘modern, large-scale wind turbines generate infrasound levels significantly higher than
those reported for older, smaller turbines.’
However, the current legal framework, and especially Directive 2002/49/EC relating to the assessment and management of
environmental noise, does not take into account this new scientific data (2).
1.
In light of these new scientific findings, does the Commission intend to revise Directive 2002/49/EC relating to the
assessment and management of environmental noise in order to include the effects of infrasound emitted by wind turbines?
2.
Does the Commission plan to support research, including through EU-funded programmes, aimed at developing
instruments allowing noise and infrasound pollution linked to wind turbines to be measured and proven?
3.
Does the Commission intend to impose harmonised thresholds at EU level for noise and infrasound emissions, given the
potential impact of these emissions on public health among people living nearby?
Submitted: 6.1.2026
Answer given by Ms Roswall on behalf of the European Commission
(18 February 2026)
The Environmental Noise Directive (END) (1) is the main EU legislative instrument for addressing excessive noise pollution
mainly caused by transport traffic, as well as from industrial activities listed in Annex I of the Industrial Emissions Directive
(IED) (2).
As electricity generation from wind turbines is not listed in the Annex I of IED, there are no specific noise requirements for
them under the END.
Wind projects (3) are subject to an Environmental Impact Assessment (4) before authorisation, which includes a description of
the emission of noise, and of the measures envisaged to prevent, reduce or, if possible, offset any adverse effect.
Member States are required, every five years, to adopt strategic noise maps showing noise exposure from major sources (5). In
this process, the END refers to the use of A-weighted equivalent sound levels as primary regulatory metrics in line with the
guidelines of the World Health Organisation (WHO) (6).
It is however noted that wind turbines generate infrasound or lower frequencies of sound than traffic sources which may not be
fully addressed by standard noise metrics.
As outlined in 2023 Implementation Report (7) and the Zero Pollution Mid-Term Review (8), the Commission is committed to
improving the implementation of the END.

title: Commission actions to level the playing field in the Horizon Europe programme
text:
QUESTION

PE782.737v01-00
Question for written answer E-000020/2026
to the Commission
Rule 144
Piotr Müller (ECR)
Subject:
Commission actions to level the playing field in the Horizon Europe programme
Horizon Europe statistics show that there are still significant and persistent differences
between Member States in accessing prestigious research grants, despite the functioning of
the Widening instruments. Applicants from central and eastern Europe continue to have a
lower success rate and a large share of the funds is concentrated in a limited number of
institutions from a handful of countries. There are also public concerns about possible
unconscious biases in assessment processes, inadequate representation of experts from
Widening countries on assessment panels and the disproportionate weight given to
institutional reputation at the expense of the actual quality and potential of projects. At the
same time, there is a lack of clear indicators to assess whether the Commission’s current
actions effectively reduce these disparities.
In light of the above:
1.
Is the Commission planning to carry out an independent audit of the procedures for
evaluating proposals in Horizon Europe, including an analysis of possible unconscious
biases and the composition of expert panels in relation to representation from Widening
countries?
2.
Is the Commission considering adapting the evaluation criteria for European Research
Council grants in order to strengthen the weight given to projects’ quality and novelty,
while decreasing that given to institutional reputation?
3.
Is the Commission analysing the introduction of systemic solutions, including
mechanisms based on national envelopes or similar instruments, that would foster more
sustainable access to research funding?
Submitted: 6.1.2026

--- ANSWER ---

(English version)
Question for written answer E-000020/26
to the Commission
Piotr Müller (ECR)
(6 January 2026)
Subject: Commission actions to level the playing field in the Horizon Europe programme
Horizon Europe statistics show that there are still significant and persistent differences between Member States in accessing
prestigious research grants, despite the functioning of the Widening instruments. Applicants from central and eastern Europe
continue to have a lower success rate and a large share of the funds is concentrated in a limited number of institutions from a
handful of countries. There are also public concerns about possible unconscious biases in assessment processes, inadequate
representation of experts from Widening countries on assessment panels and the disproportionate weight given to institutional
reputation at the expense of the actual quality and potential of projects. At the same time, there is a lack of clear indicators to
assess whether the Commission’s current actions effectively reduce these disparities.
In light of the above:
1.
Is the Commission planning to carry out an independent audit of the procedures for evaluating proposals in Horizon
Europe, including an analysis of possible unconscious biases and the composition of expert panels in relation to
representation from Widening countries?
2.
Is the Commission considering adapting the evaluation criteria for European Research Council grants in order to
strengthen the weight given to projects’ quality and novelty, while decreasing that given to institutional reputation?
3.
Is the Commission analysing the introduction of systemic solutions, including mechanisms based on national envelopes
or similar instruments, that would foster more sustainable access to research funding?
Submitted: 6.1.2026
Answer given by Ms Zaharieva on behalf of the European Commission
(25 March 2026)
The Commission implements a robust evaluation process for Horizon Europe designed to ensure equal treatment, fairness,
transparency, and impartiality.
Proposals are assessed by external independent experts who collaborate to reach a consensus, which helps mitigate individual
biases. In two-stage calls, first-stage proposals are evaluated blindly where possible, providing an additional safeguard against
bias.
Evaluator panels reflect geographical diversity, including representatives from widening countries. An independent study (1)
concluded that the evaluation system in Horizon Europe is broadly fair.
The Commission is committed to continuous improvement, focusing on maintaining the same high quality in the process, with
particular attention to the inclusion of widening countries.
The European Research Council (ERC) uses scientific excellence as the sole award criterion for assessing proposals. In 2024,
the ERC (2) introduced further reforms to reduce bias and to ensure that the excellence of the research project carries more
weight than the applicant’s track record.
The new Horizon Europe proposal (3) strives to align European, national, and regional priorities, to strengthen research and
innovation ecosystems by creating close links with the European Competitiveness Fund proposal (4) and coordinated
investments through the proposed new National and Regional Partnership Plans (NRPPs) (5).

Fabio De Masi (NI)
(6 January 2026)
Subject: Secret peace plans for the conflict in Ukraine
According to press reports, secret peace plans for the conflict in Ukraine were drawn up before the 28-point plan (1). The
reports state that the German Government was already aware of an ‘Istanbul Plan’ on 4 November 2025. German and European
diplomacy’s response to this has been cautious.
1.
Was the plan discussed at Council level?
2.
Were Member States aware of the plan?
Submitted: 6.1.2026
Reply
(30 March 2026)
It is not for the Council to comment on articles appearing in the press. As to Member States’ awareness of any plan, we would
invite the Honourable Member to address his queries to the Member States in question.

title: Application of common agricultural policy income support instruments in cases of  force majeure  due to severe climate events
text:
QUESTION

PE782.739v01-00
Question for written answer E-000022/2026
to the Commission
Rule 144
Radan Kanev (PPE)
Subject:
Application of common agricultural policy income support instruments in cases of
force majeure due to severe climate events
In Bulgaria in 2025, severe frost and freezing led, in some cases, to the total destruction of
fruit crops, leaving affected farmers without marketable production or income. The only
support provided was partial compensation of production costs under a national State aid
scheme, which does not address income loss and may worsen farmers’ situation following
force majeure events.
As per the national guidelines for compensating crop losses caused by adverse climatic events
in 2025, areas receiving such aid are excluded from eligibility for coupled income support for
the same crops and areas in Campaign 20251.
Regulation (EU) 2021/21162, notably Articles 3 and 59(5), requires Member States to take
account of force majeure and exceptional circumstances and to ensure that farmers are not
penalised for losses resulting from events beyond their control.
1.
Does the Commission consider such exclusions from coupled income support
compatible with Articles 3 and 59(5) of Regulation (EU) 2021/2116 in cases of
recognised force majeure?
2.
How does the Commission ensure that national common agricultural policy rules
comply with EU law regarding force majeure and exceptional circumstances?
Submitted: 7.1.2026
1
Implementing guidelines for the State aid scheme “Compensation for damage to agricultural crops caused by
adverse climatic events which can be equated to natural disasters” – Campaign 2025 (latest version,
additional resource). State Fund “Agriculture”, Republic of Bulgaria,
https://www.dfz.bg/documents/d/guest/ukazania_kompensirane-zagubi_prez-2025_dopalnitelen-resurs.
2
Regulation (EU) 2021/2116 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 2 December 2021 on the
financing, management and monitoring of the common agricultural policy and repealing Regulation (EU) No
1306/2013 (OJ L 435, 6.12.2021, p. 187, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2021/2116/oj).

--- ANSWER ---

(English version)
Question for written answer E-000022/26
to the Commission
Radan Kanev (PPE)
(7 January 2026)
Subject: Application of common agricultural policy income support instruments in cases of force majeure due to severe climate
events
In Bulgaria in 2025, severe frost and freezing led, in some cases, to the total destruction of fruit crops, leaving affected farmers
without marketable production or income. The only support provided was partial compensation of production costs under a
national state aid scheme, which does not address income loss and may worsen farmers’ situation following force majeure
events.
As per the national guidelines for compensating crop losses caused by adverse climatic events in 2025, areas receiving such aid
are excluded from eligibility for coupled income support for the same crops and areas in Campaign 2025 (1).
Regulation (EU) 2021/2116 (2), notably Articles 3 and 59(5), requires Member States to take account of force majeure and
exceptional circumstances and to ensure that farmers are not penalised for losses resulting from events beyond their control.
1.
Does the Commission consider such exclusions from coupled income support compatible with Articles 3 and 59(5) of
Regulation (EU) 2021/2116 in cases of recognised force majeure?
2.
How does the Commission ensure that national common agricultural policy rules comply with EU law regarding force
majeure and exceptional circumstances?
Submitted: 7.1.2026
Answer given by Mr Hansen on behalf of the European Commission
(11 March 2026)
Coupled income support addresses structural difficulties that certain targeted sectors face; it does not address income losses due
to severe meteorological events.
Nevertheless, force majeure events may exempt a producer from certain legal consequences that would otherwise occur in an
instance of non-compliance with coupled income support rules.
For example, in accordance with Articles 59, 84 and 88 of Regulation (EU) 2021/2116 (1), no penalties are to be imposed and
the beneficiary is to retain the right to receive common agricultural policy support where the non-compliance is due to force
majeure or exceptional circumstances in accordance with Article 3 of the same Regulation. This is relevant in cases such as a
severe natural disaster or severe meteorological event gravely affecting the holding.
Whereas the application of force majeure is the responsibility of Member States, Member States should take the decision to
apply force majeure based on relevant evidence and in light of Union agricultural law.
Force majeure is an exception to the general rule of strict respect of obligations. Normally applied on a case-by-case basis, in
cases of severe meteorological events that gravely affect a well-determined area, Member States may consider that a whole area
is concerned, where it is clear that the farmers in the area are affected by an abnormal event whose consequences could not be
prevented with all due care.
Member States need, however, to determine the area at stake and the population affected by the event, in a manner that
reasonably allows the presumption that the conditions of force majeure are individually met by the farmers concerned (2).

agricultural policy and repealing Regulation (EU) No 1306/2013 (OJ L 435, 6.12.2021, p. 187, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2021/2116/oj).
